node.label: Aldo Leopold
node.date_label: Land ethic and ecological interpretation of history · A Sand County Almanac 1949
node.description: A forester, wildlife ecologist and conservationist, not a historian, whose posthumous A Sand County Almanac (1949) set out a 'land ethic' that 'changes the role of Homo sapiens from conqueror of the land-community to plain member and citizen of it'. In the same essay he wrote that an 'ecological interpretation of history' shows that 'many historical events, hitherto explained solely in terms of human enterprise, were actually biotic interactions between people and land', and took as his example the Kentucky canelands that became bluegrass under 'the cow, plow, fire, and axe of the pioneer'. He asked: 'Is history taught in this spirit? It will be, once the concept of land as a community really penetrates our intellectual life.' Environmental historians later cited the call: Worster (1988) wrote that Leopold 'projected such an alliance' between history and ecology, and Cronon (1993) described the field's subject as 'the history recorded in Aldo Leopold’s tree rings'.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Aldo Leopold (1887–1948); A Sand County Almanac, and Sketches Here and There (1949), especially 'Good Oak' and 'The Land Ethic'. Readings: Nash, Wilderness and the American Mind (1967), chapter 'Aldo Leopold: Prophet'; Worster, 'Doing Environmental History' (1988) and 'Transformations of the Earth' (1990); Cronon, 'The Uses of Environmental History' (1993) and History 901 syllabus (1994). Later readings: Wynn (2001); MacEachern (2002); Cronon's afterword to Changes in the Land (2003).
node.scope_note: This entry presents Leopold as a precursor whose writing environmental historians cited, not as a historian and not as the founder of environmental history. 'The Land Ethic' and 'Good Oak' are read in two unpaginated transcriptions (the 1966 enlarged Oxford text and an excerpt of the 1949 essay); the 1949 page of the history passage (p. 205) is the one Worster (1990, n. 1) and Wynn (2001, n. 55) both cite. Worster's 1988 essay dates 'the idea of environmental history' to the 1970s, the global-predicament conferences and the environmental movement, not to Leopold. His 1990 essay, read only in Portuguese translation, cautions that the Kentucky case is more complicated than Leopold's example and needs more than a simple environmental determinism, and adds that bluegrass was a European import, which Leopold had said was not known. Cronon's 1993 uses are echoes of a moral and literary voice, not a borrowed method. Canadian writing differs: MacEachern (2002, p. 219) faults a history of Ontario conservation for assuming, without evidence, that Leopold 'was being read by Canadians, let alone influencing them' (a remark about naturalists of the 1950s, not about historians), and Wynn (2001, p. 145), a historical geographer, urges geographers to 'respond to Leopold’s call' and observes: 'Few have done so'.

proposed_edges.relationship: Environmental historians cite Leopold's call for 'an ecological interpretation of history' (1949) as a precedent for allying history with ecology, and his essays as a moral and literary voice
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Leopold's text, 'The Land Ethic', A Sand County Almanac (1949), read in two unpaginated transcriptions: 'That man is, in fact, only a member of a biotic team is shown by an ecological interpretation of history. Many historical events, hitherto explained solely in terms of human enterprise, were actually biotic interactions between people and land. The characteristics of the land determined the facts quite as potently as the characteristics of the men who lived on it.' After the Kentucky example: 'Is history taught in this spirit? It will be, once the concept of land as a community really penetrates our intellectual life.' Worster (1990, n. 1) and Wynn (2001, n. 55) cite the history passage at p. 205 of the 1949 edition; a paginated 1949 copy was not seen. In-period readings by historians. (1) Worster, 'Doing Environmental History' (1988), abridged reprint read (Merchant reader, 2012, pp. 2–9; reprint pages): 'Take away plant ecology and environmental history loses its foundation, its coherence, its first step' (p. 5); some scholars speak of 'ecological history' or 'historical ecology', meaning 'to insist on a tighter alliance with the science. Some years back the scientist and conservationist Aldo Leopold projected such an alliance when he spoke of “an ecological interpretation of history.”' (pp. 5–6). He then retells the Kentucky example and quotes Leopold's question about 'the plant succession inherent in this dark and bloody ground' (p. 6). (2) Worster, 'Transformations of the Earth', JAH 76 (1990), read only in Portuguese translation (Ambiente & Sociedade, 2002–03): the essay opens with Leopold, who 'reivindicou uma “interpretação ecológica da História”', and continues 'Levou algum tempo para os historiadores darem atenção ao conselho de Leopold, mas finalmente o campo da história ambiental começou a ganhar forma' (p. 23; gloss: it took historians some time to heed Leopold's advice, but the field of environmental history finally began to take shape). The English wording is unchecked. (3) Cronon, 'The Uses of Environmental History' (1993), read in full: 'Environmental history tries to reconstruct the endless layers of change that we and the earth have traced upon each other. It is the history recorded in Aldo Leopold’s tree rings, the history recorded by the marks of his saw upon the good oak as he cut it down' (p. 19; n. 32, p. 22: 'The echo here is that of Leopold’s “Good Oak,” Sand County Almanac, 6-18'); n. 11 (p. 21): 'At this and several other points in this essay, I trust that readers will hear my echoes of Aldo Leopold's Sand County Almanac'. (4) Cronon's History 901 syllabus (Fall 1994) assigns 'Good Oak' in the session 'Reading the Landscape, Part I' (p. 4) and 'Thinking Like a Mountain' with Part IV, 'The Upshot', beside Nash's Wilderness and the American Mind (p. 6). (5) Nash's Wilderness and the American Mind (1967), checked at contents level only, gives him a chapter, 'Aldo Leopold: Prophet'. Bounded: Worster dates 'the idea of environmental history' to the 1970s and the environmental movement (1988, reprint p. 3), and in 1990 warns that the Kentucky facts need more than 'uma forma simples de determinismo ambiental' (p. 24; gloss: a simple form of environmental determinism). Later reading, not evidence for this edge: Cronon's 2003 afterword (pp. 174–175) recalls 'reading the landscape' workshops 'modeled on a famous course taught by Aldo Leopold as early as the 1930s' and calls the Almanac 'no less a meditation on the history of human interactions with the American land'.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: No environment strand fits. sauer_teaching_reception is Cronon's 1994 assignment of Sauer; wilderness_culture and the wilderness strands concern Cronon's 1995 essay and its critics; agriculture_capitalism and malin_adaptation_debate concern the Dust Bowl. The geography strand leopold_landscape is on the other node. A reviewer could add an environment strand at release, for example 'An ecological interpretation of history' (person_ids aldo_leopold, donald_worster, william_cronon; works: Almanac 1949; Worster 1988, 1990; Cronon 1993), resting on this edge's sources.

edges_considered_not_proposed.reason: He has a geography roster row and the strand leopold_landscape, but both rest on Cronon's 2003 afterword, a later reading about Cronon's own Wisconsin schooling. That passage names geographers (Lawrence Martin, Glenn Trewartha, Andrew Hill Clark) among his teachers but does not say that geographers drew on Leopold. No in-period text read shows geographers taking him up. The one geographer's text read, Wynn (2001, pp. 144–145), urges historical geographers to 'respond to Leopold’s call' and says 'Few have done so'; interest in 'such an ecological perspective on human affairs has been slow to take root'. An influence edge to geography would claim what that text denies. Not proposed; the roster row and strand stay without edge_id.

The strongest evidence names two individual historians. Their person entries are being drafted in parallel for 1.131 and do not yet exist as nodes, so person-to-person edges cannot be validated here. If both entries are accepted, the editor may prefer aldo_leopold → donald_worster (1988, 1990) and aldo_leopold → william_cronon (1993, 1994) to the field-level edge, or add them beside it.

new_sources.title: Donald Worster, “Doing Environmental History,” appendix to Worster, ed., The Ends of the Earth: Perspectives on Modern Environmental History (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1988), 289–307; abridged reprint in Carolyn Merchant, ed., Major Problems in American Environmental History, 3rd ed. (Boston: Wadsworth, Cengage Learning, 2012), ch. 1.
new_sources.citation: Donald Worster, “Doing Environmental History,” in Worster, ed., The Ends of the Earth (Cambridge University Press, 1988), 289–307 (doi:10.1017/CBO9781139173599.014); abridged in Merchant, ed., Major Problems in American Environmental History, 3rd ed. (2012), 2–9.

verification.note: Abridged reprint read in full in the chapter 1 PDF posted for UC Berkeley ESPM 160 (Merchant reader, 3rd ed., © 2012 Wadsworth, Cengage Learning; ISBN 978-0-495-91242-2, from the same course's contents PDF). The reprint's credit line gives the original as The Ends of the Earth (Cambridge University Press, 1988), pp. 289–299, 301–303, 305–306, with ellipses for omissions. Page numbers quoted are the reprint's. Crossref 10.1017/CBO9781139173599.014: 'Appendix: Doing Environmental History', The Ends of the Earth, pp. 289–308. Reprint p. 3: 'The idea of environmental history first appeared in the 1970s, as conferences on the global predicament were taking place and popular environmentalist movements were gathering momentum in several countries.' p. 5: 'Take away plant ecology and environmental history loses its foundation, its coherence, its first step.' pp. 5–6: some scholars speak of 'ecological history' or 'historical ecology'; 'They mean to insist on a tighter alliance with the science. Some years back the scientist and conservationist Aldo Leopold projected such an alliance when he spoke of “an ecological interpretation of history.”' p. 6: the Kentucky canebrake and bluegrass example, and the quoted question 'What if … the plant succession inherent in this dark and bloody ground had, under the impact of forces, given us some worthless sedge, shrub, or weed?' (Leopold's text reads 'under the impact of these forces'; the difference is the reprint's or Worster's). The original 1988 pagination of these passages was not seen; the omitted original pages (299–301, 303–305, 306–307) were not read.

new_sources.scope_note: In-period programmatic essay by a historian: Leopold as precedent for an alliance of history and ecology.

new_sources.title: Donald Worster, “Transformations of the Earth: Toward an Agroecological Perspective in History,” Journal of American History 76, no. 4 (March 1990): 1087–1106; read in Portuguese translation, “Transformações da terra: para uma perspectiva agroecológica na história,” Ambiente & Sociedade 5, no. 2–6, no. 1 (2002–2003): 23–44.
new_sources.citation: Donald Worster, “Transformations of the Earth: Toward an Agroecological Perspective in History,” Journal of American History 76:4 (1990): 1087–1106, doi:10.2307/2936586; Portuguese translation by Maria Clara Abalo Ferraz de Andrade, Ambiente & Sociedade (2002–03): 23–44.

verification.note: The English original was not seen (JSTOR blocked; no open copy found). Crossref 10.2307/2936586 confirms JAH 76:4 (March 1990), first page 1087. The Portuguese translation was read in the PDF of orgprints eprint 20347 (Worster_transformações.pdf), whose first-page note says the article was first published in the Journal of American History in March 1990. Quoted from the translation: p. 23, 'Há quarenta anos atrás, um homem sábio e visionário, o conservacionista e biólogo da vida selvagem, Aldo Leopold, de Wisconsin, reivindicou uma “interpretação ecológica da História”, pela qual propunha usar as idéias e a pesquisa do emergente campo da ecologia para ajudar a explicar porque os fatos que constituem o passado desenvolveram-se da maneira como os conhecemos'; 'Levou algum tempo para os historiadores darem atenção ao conselho de Leopold, mas finalmente o campo da história ambiental começou a ganhar forma e seus praticantes estão tentando construir a partir de sua iniciativa.' p. 24: 'os fatos no caso são mais complicados do que Leopold poderia ter explorado nos limites de seu ensaio, e eles exigem mais do que uma forma simples de determinismo ambiental, que é o que um leitor menos atento poderia encontrar em seu exemplo'; Kentucky bluegrass 'não era uma espécie nativa, mas uma importação européia', followed by Crosby's 'imperialismo ecológico'. Notes, p. 42: n. 1 cites Leopold, A Sand County Almanac, and Sketches Here and There (1949; reprinted New York, 1987), p. 205; n. 3 says Leopold knew the story was more complex and quotes him (p. 206) that 'we do not even know' where bluegrass came from. English glosses in the atlas are the editor's, not Worster's words. A Bowdoin course guide paraphrasing the essay was seen and not used.

new_sources.scope_note: In-period programmatic essay: Leopold's call as the field's opening precedent, with Worster's caution against a determinist reading. Translation only; the English wording must be checked before it is quoted in English.

new_sources.title: William Cronon, “The Uses of Environmental History,” Environmental History Review 17, no. 3 (Fall 1993): 1–22.
new_sources.citation: William Cronon, “The Uses of Environmental History,” Environmental History Review 17:3 (1993): 1–22.

verification.note: Scanned PDF from the author's site, read in full through OCR (pp. 1–22, notes included); superscript note numbers are not reliably readable in the OCR. p. 19: 'Environmental history tries to reconstruct the endless layers of change that we and the earth have traced upon each other. It is the history recorded in Aldo Leopold’s tree rings, the history recorded by the marks of his saw upon the good oak as he cut it down, the history recorded by the memories in the hatted head with its shadow on the stump'; n. 32 (p. 22): 'The echo here is that of Leopold’s “Good Oak,” Sand County Almanac, 6-18.' n. 11 (p. 21): 'At this and several other points in this essay, I trust that readers will hear my echoes of Aldo Leopold's Sand County Almanac (New York: Oxford University Press, 1949), 224-25.' By note order, n. 11 falls on p. 7, where some environmental historians measure 'usefulness' 'by whether or not it contributes to the health and integrity of natural systems'. It places the field's origins in 'the political movement that helped spawn it' (p. 2).

new_sources.scope_note: In-period presidential address: Leopold as a moral and literary voice for the field.

new_sources.title: Graeme Wynn, “Thinking About Mountains, Valleys and Solitudes: Historical Geography and the New Atlantic History,” Acadiensis 31, no. 1 (Autumn 2001): 129–145.
new_sources.citation: Graeme Wynn, “Thinking About Mountains, Valleys and Solitudes: Historical Geography and the New Atlantic History,” Acadiensis 31:1 (2001): 129–145.

verification.note: PDF from the UNB OJS site; pp. 142–145 and notes 48–55 read, the rest searched for Leopold. The title 'gestures to Aldo Leopold' (p. 129). pp. 142–143: Leopold's 'Good Oak' allegory of saw and wedge as 'fragrant little chips of history' (n. 48: Almanac, New York, 1949, pp. 6–18). p. 144: Leopold's 'land ethic', which 'enlarges the boundaries of the community to include soils, waters, plants and animals, or collectively: the land' (n. 54: Almanac pp. 129–30, 204); 'Yet interest in such an ecological perspective on human affairs has been slow to take root.' p. 145: 'In the United States and elsewhere the vigorous new field of environmental history has grown from this conjuncture. In Canada, by contrast, the response has been faltering'; 'there is irony in the scant attention that geographers have paid this element of their “birthright”'; historical geographers are well placed 'to respond to Leopold’s call to recognize that “many historical events, hitherto explained solely in terms of human enterprise, were actually biotic interactions between people and land”' (n. 55: Almanac p. 205); 'Few have done so'.

new_sources.scope_note: Later reading (2001) by a Canadian historical geographer: Leopold's call as unanswered in geography and in Canada. Not evidence for any edge.

new_sources.title: Alan MacEachern, “Voices Crying in the Wilderness: Recent Works in Canadian Environmental History,” Acadiensis 31, no. 2 (2002): 215–226.
new_sources.citation: Alan MacEachern, “Voices Crying in the Wilderness: Recent Works in Canadian Environmental History,” Acadiensis 31:2 (2002): 215–226.

verification.note: Review essay read in the PDF from the UNB OJS site (12 pp.; OJS metadata: first page 215, dated 2002); pp. 215–216 and 219–220 read closely. p. 219, on George Warecki's Protecting Ontario's Wilderness: 'The American model at times seems accepted as the normative one that the Canadian case should follow. For example, while discussing a 1958 FON document, the author breaks off to explain the significance of American Aldo Leopold’s land ethic to the field of ecology in the 1950s. … Yet there is no evidence here, nor the next four times the ecologist is mentioned, that Leopold was being read by Canadians, let alone influencing them.' The remark concerns Ontario naturalists of the 1950s (the FON), not Canadian historians. pp. 215–216 name Nash, Cronon, Worster, Merchant, White and Pyne as the US 'front rank', and p. 216 advises against 'a slavish adherence to an American model'.

new_sources.scope_note: Later reading (2002), Canadian: caution against assuming Leopold's influence in Canada. Scope note only.

leopold_almanac.note: Text of 'The Land Ethic' and 'Good Oak' read for the 1.131 person entry in two unpaginated transcriptions: an accessible-media text of the 1966 enlarged Oxford edition on the Internet Archive (item sand-county-almanac-with-essays-on-conservation-from-round-river-by-aldo-leopold; contents give 'Good Oak' p. 6 and 'The Land Ethic' p. 237 of that edition), and a transcription of 'The Land Ethic' headed 1949 (faculty.lsu.edu/kharms/files/leopold_1949.pdf). The two agree on the passages quoted. 'The land ethic simply enlarges the boundaries of the community to include soils, waters, plants, and animals, or collectively: the land.' 'In short, a land ethic changes the role of Homo sapiens from conqueror of the land-community to plain member and citizen of it.' 'That man is, in fact, only a member of a biotic team is shown by an ecological interpretation of history. Many historical events, hitherto explained solely in terms of human enterprise, were actually biotic interactions between people and land. The characteristics of the land determined the facts quite as potently as the characteristics of the men who lived on it.' The Kentucky cane-lands, 'when subjected to the particular mixture of forces represented by the cow, plow, fire, and axe of the pioneer, became bluegrass'; 'we do not even know where the bluegrass came from'; 'In short, the plant succession steered the course of history'; 'Is history taught in this spirit? It will be, once the concept of land as a community really penetrates our intellectual life.' 'Good Oak': 'Fragrant little chips of history spewed from the saw cut'; 'The three tools are requisite to good oak, and to good history.' 1949 pages, from others' citations only: history passage p. 205 (Worster 1990, n. 1; Wynn 2001, n. 55); bluegrass origin p. 206 (Worster 1990, n. 3); community boundaries p. 204 (Wynn 2001, n. 54); 'Good Oak' pp. 6–18 (Cronon 1993, n. 32; Wynn 2001, n. 48). The Almanac's 1933 forerunner, 'The Conservation Ethic' (Journal of Forestry 31:6, 634–643, doi:10.1093/jof/31.6.634), was not read.

cronon_environment_syllabus_1994.note: Re-read in the Internet Archive capture web.archive.org/web/20201021214718id_/ of the history.wisc.edu PDF (six pages; the original URL now returns 404). Leopold assignments: p. 2, the book list gives 'Aldo Leopold, Sand County Almanac, QH81 L56 1966' (the enlarged edition) beside Nash's Wilderness and the American Mind; p. 4, 28 September, 'READING THE LANDSCAPE, PART I': 'Aldo Leopold, “Good Oak,” A Sand County Almanac, 6-19'; p. 6, 16 November, 'A SPECIAL AFFECTION FOR THINGS WILD': 'Roderick Nash, Wilderness and the American Mind, 1-7, 96-199' and 'Aldo Leopold, A Sand County Almanac, 137-41, 237-95. (If you're using another edition, these are the essays entitled “Thinking Like a Mountain,” and Part IV of the Book, “The Upshot.”)'. An assignment shows teaching use, not assent.

cronon_changes_afterword.note: Re-read for the 1.131 Leopold entry. The Leopold passages are on pp. 174–175 (the existing note's pp. 173–175 range covers them): the 'reading the landscape' workshops at the university arboretum 'were in fact modeled on a famous course taught by Aldo Leopold as early as the 1930s'; the Almanac, 'usually read today as one of the greatest twentieth-century contributions to American nature writing', 'is no less a meditation on the history of human interactions with the American land'; the teachers he names include the geographers Lawrence Martin, Glenn Trewartha and Andrew Hill Clark, who 'may not have called themselves environmental historians'; his high-school reconstruction of presettlement vegetation was in 'the county where Aldo Leopold's famous “Shack” is located' (p. 175).

citation_evidence.works: A Sand County Almanac (3 dissertations; 2 of them listed it as a primary source); 'The Conservation Ethic' in The River of the Mother of God (1, primary source); Game Management (1933) (1, the 1997 Saskatchewan thesis on government–Indian relations).
citation_evidence.idea_vs_content: Not listed: 4 citing PhDs is far below the script's 40-PhD threshold.
citation_evidence.caveat: Bibliographies record consultation, not influence. Two of four dissertations treat the Almanac as a primary source, which fits the Canadian self-accounts that read Leopold as a historical actor rather than a model. Low counts say more about Canadian History PhD reading than about Leopold.
